title: Fake news: the impact of the internet on population health
screen_reason: The abstract reports a share of survey respondents who say they received misinformation: of 1,195 respondents, 89.4% had received fake news. 'Received' is explicitly within the RECALL definition, the denominator is stated, and the study is a descriptive cross-sectional survey whose stated aim includes determining the frequency of fake health news. Only the abstract is available, so nothing beyond it could be checked.

estimates.platform: self-reported receipt of fake health news online; abstract names Facebook and WhatsApp as the main means of receipt
estimates.measure_type: % of survey respondents who reported having received fake news (health)
estimates.value_raw: A large part of the sample (89.4%) had received fake news
estimates.denominator: 1,195 respondents to an online questionnaire distributed via social media platforms by snowball sampling in 2019
estimates.definition: Respondent answered that they had received fake news; the questionnaire item wording, the recall window and any definition given to respondents are not reported in the abstract.
estimates.misinfo_def: Not reported in the abstract; the paper refers only to "fake health news" / "fake news".
estimates.source_quote: A large part of the sample (89.4%) had received fake news, and the main means of receipt were Facebook and WhatsApp.
estimates.page_loc: Abstract, Results section (abstract-only record; no page numbers available)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Respondent self-report on a questionnaire; no external verification and no definition of fake news supplied to respondents is described in the abstract.
estimates.moderator_quote: A descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted through the virtual distribution of questionnaires on social media platforms in 2019 by using the snowball technique. The questionnaire collected information regarding sociodemographics, means used to clarify doubts about health, implementation of information obtained through the Internet, receipt of fake news, and means of transmission of fake news.
estimates.notes: ABSTRACT-ONLY EXTRACTION - the value (89.4%) and denominator (1,195) are verbatim, but four moderators could not be verified and an adjudicator with the full text should re-check them: (a) COUNTRY is never named in the abstract, so country_norm is coded 'Global' per the schema rule for unspecified geography even though this is plainly a single-country convenience sample; (b) the questionnaire item wording and recall window are unknown, so breadth is coded 'false' from the label 'fake news' alone; (c) sampling_frame coded 'convenience' from the stated snowball recruitment on social media - a self-selected online sample of people already active on the platforms where fake news circulates, which very likely inflates 89.4%; (d) topic coded health_other from 'fake health news', but the item may have asked about fake news in general.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) Only the abstract was available (text_status abstract_only), so the results tables, the exact item wording, the country and any subgroup breakdowns could not be seen. (2) Other abstract percentages are not misinformation measures and were not extracted: 53% had followed Internet guidance without consulting a health professional; the resources most used for health questions were a physician (78%) and Google (51%). (3) The abstract says the main means of receipt were Facebook and WhatsApp but gives no per-platform percentages, so no platform-split rows are possible - the full text may contain them. (4) 'Means of transmission of fake news' was also collected, which suggests a self-reported SHARING (recall_subtype sharing) item may exist in the full text; no number for it appears in the abstract. (5) The country must be recovered from the full text before this row is used in any country-level analysis.

rob.design: Descriptive cross-sectional online survey, 2019: questionnaires distributed virtually on social media platforms using snowball sampling (self-selected, non-probability), n = 1,195 respondents; no sampling frame, no response rate and no country reported in the abstract; measures were self-reported (sociodemographics, sources used for health questions, acting on internet information, receipt of fake news, means of transmission); analysis by means/SD for quantitative variables, frequencies/percentages for categorical variables, chi-square and Fisher's exact tests. No coding procedure or reliability statistics are applicable, since misinformation receipt is entirely self-reported and undefined in the abstract.
